item.title: From Tense to Confident Parenting
item.description:
Parenting

From Tense to Confident Parenting

A visual guide to help shift from child-focused worry to confident parenting.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Focus on changing your parenting responses, not trying to change your child.
  • Self-awareness helps parents move from anxious reactivity to confident leadership.
  • Less over-functioning gives children more room to develop confidence and responsibility.
  • Balanced parenting combines warmth and connection with clear boundaries and leadership.

In my recent book, The Parenting Paradox, I introduce stories of parents recovering balance in their parenting by making themselves and their reactions their number one project rather than trying to change their children. This is the paradoxical path of developing parent confidence and loving leadership for children.

In this post, I’m sharing a short excerpt from this section, followed by a visual diagram I've created to bring this paradox to life.

A Mindset Shift: Reduce Attention on Our Children, Increase Attention on Ourselves

Any change of direction starts with a mindset shift. Techniques and strategies without a clear understanding of the thinking behind them won’t bring sustainable change. The mindset shift for parents is about a change of focus and attention. The focus of our energy is best invested in ourselves as parents and what we can change, rather than trying to fix or change our child. It might sound somewhat radical that we reduce our attention on our children and increase our attention on ourselves as parents. Not attending to self-interest but to our growth in awareness. In this way, the parent and what we can adjust becomes the project, not the child.

I wonder if you’re asking yourself if such a shift is possible. It feels like so many of our parenting instincts are deeply attuned to protecting and watching over our children. All the messages about attuning and attaching to children add to parents, making children the main project. The key is to manage those good and natural instincts and not let them get the better of you. When instincts start running the show, the balance gets lost, and the investment in our children prevents us from developing ourselves as parents. Parents who can cultivate self-awareness are best positioned to provide a growth-enhancing environment for their children.”

Here’s a diagram to illustrate the counterintuitive journey of change grounded in differentiation-based parenting. (part of Bowen family systems theory) See if it helps to bring this idea to greater clarity.

Two Houses: From Tense to Confident Parenting

Source: Parent Hope Project

On the left, the Tense Parenting House shows a parent caught in cycles of worry and reactivity. The energy flows toward changing the child—driven by fear and the belief that the solution lies in fixing the child. Attention toward the child’s weakness is leading the parenting. This reactive focus often leads to over-functioning, in which the parent conveys, in words and actions, “You need to change.” “You will comply.” This approach, though rooted in care, easily creates dependency. We see it in the words rising from the chimney: “Dependent Reactor”—a child who, shaped by worried over-involvement, cannot access their capacity.

On the right, the Confident Parenting House tells a different story. Here, the energy is directed toward the parents’ posture and presence: “Change Me.” Awareness of parenting patterns leads the effort. The parent is no less loving, but their love is expressed through observation, curiosity, and acting from their space of influence. This parent gives space, connects without fusing, and leads by applying curiosity to observing their patterns and growing their maturity. They shift from a “you” stance to an “I” position—“Here’s what I am willing to do and what I am not willing to do.” The result? A child who becomes an “Independent Relator”—emotionally equipped to engage the world with growing confidence and responsibility.

We parents become, in essence, loving leaders in the family—grounded, responsible, and capable of providing structure while offering warmth. This is balanced parenting—not too much support that fosters dependence, not too little that leaves a child adrift, but just enough support from a parent’s values to create the conditions for a child’s maturity to emerge.

The Surprise in Moving from Being Child-Led To Parent-Led

“At the heart of this parenting pathway lies a powerful paradox: the more we anxiously focus on our children—trying to protect, perfect, or preempt their every challenge—the more we unintentionally undermine their ability to mature. And in doing so, we lose the space we need to grow our parenting awareness. The turning point comes when we stop managing our children as projects and instead focus on how we show up in our relationships with them. Rather than hovering, rescuing, or absorbing our children’s distress, we learn to hold ourselves well in the face of their struggles.”

This shift can help us move from tense to confident parents, and isn’t that something every carer aspires to?

item.title: Stop Trying to Feel so Connected to Your Partner
item.description:
Relationships

Stop Trying to Feel so Connected to Your Partner

Moments of intimacy are not how love should be measured.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • We are fed the idea that a good relationship means you regulate your distress together and are fully seen.
  • Making connection a constant requirement is risky: More mundane times are evidence something is wrong.
  • A relationship centred on loyalty, kindness, and shared childcare can be a more realistic vision of success.

Intimacy, attunement, emotional responsiveness: The language varies, but the ideal remains much the same. You should feel deeply known by your partner and connected at all times. You should understand each other, share values, regulate your distress together, and strive to be fully seen.

Connection has become one of the main ways we judge a relationship. You are encouraged to protect it, cultivate it, discuss it, and work hard to recover it. Sometimes you might even wonder if you should leave and seek it elsewhere.

Only connect?

Of course connection matters. But a good relationship cannot be a continuous series of emotionally charged encounters. A beautiful sunset is a pleasure, but you cannot sensibly expect one every evening. The trouble begins when connection becomes a constant requirement or the yardstick by which you measure everything else.

In any long-term relationship, there will be times when you feel less close to one another. A new job might mean work becomes all-consuming for a while. One of you might become ill or need to care for a relative. Money may be tight. And when you’re raising children, there are times when your entire relationship seems to consist mainly of passing the baton of shared childcare.

There is a world of difference, though, between a relationship that feels short of warmth at present and one in which warmth has gone for good. Treating every lapse as proof that the relationship is virtually over is the equivalent of assuming the garden is dead in February.

Some attempts to correct the problem can make it worse, too. Couples are often advised to devote time and effort to monitoring and restoring connection, so they book date nights, arrange a weekend in an expensive hotel, or schedule regular conversations about how close they feel.

Those efforts are not wrong. Time together can help. So can an honest conversation about what you miss. But connection is a bit like sleep—you can darken the room and put away your phone, but you cannot force it. The relationship industry is keen on promoting (and selling) card games, questions, and exercises designed to bring couples closer. Some are useful. But connection is usually a byproduct of spending time together and treating each other well. Constantly checking whether you feel it can suffocate a relationship as readily as it revives one.

I want it all

The pressure to feel connected all the time grows when we expect one relationship to meet nearly all our emotional needs. We monitor connection so anxiously because we have made our romantic relationships responsible for too much.

As psychologist Eli Finkel says, many of us now look to our relationships for personal growth and self-expression, not just for companionship and support. He calls this the all-or-nothing relationship, and it’s easy to come away with the impression that relationships built around the more modest goals of companionship, sex, and shared family life somehow fall short.

But this hierarchy is not justified. A relationship centred on loyalty, kindness, and shared childcare is not necessarily an incomplete version of something grander. Many people neither want nor need to continually assess how close they feel to their partner, let alone make constant connection their goal.

A more realistic stance can work better. Adjusting expectations does not mean giving up on your relationship—it’s a sign of maturity to accept that your partner has limits, just as you do. It leaves room for other people, too: A friend may understand the pressures of your work better, or you might prefer to talk politics with a colleague or to share a particular sense of humour with a sibling.

These connections don’t expose a hole in your relationship; they help protect it. Seeking everything from one person is risky—if they become the sole source of intimacy, stimulation, reassurance, and recognition, every time they fall short, it feels like a serious failure.

Most of us want to feel understood and cared for by a partner. But you also need to manage some feelings for yourself: to notice when you feel disconnected or disappointed and resist treating those moments as evidence that the relationship is in trouble. Resilience is not emotional withdrawal.

The wonderful everyday

Ordinary dissatisfactions are the entry price for sharing a life with somebody. The school run is sometimes stressful. There are bills to pay and disagreements about dinner. It’s annoying when your partner leaves wet towels on the bed or gets stuck at work, but it isn’t earth-shattering. You don’t have to enjoy these times, but neither are they a sign that the relationship is in trouble. Sometimes patience and understanding are what’s called for.

At other times, the ordinary stuff is lovely because someone is alongside you for the ride. They know what sort of day you’ve had and what your boss is like. They tease you when you’re taking yourself too seriously but know when to stop joking and put an arm around you. You both complain about the traffic or the neighbour’s dog. You share the small dramas of each other’s lives, know what gets under each other’s skin, and enjoy each other’s company.

When you feel less close, before wondering about the future of the relationship, ask how you treat each other. Are you still kind? Can you appreciate what is going well, listen when something matters to the other person, and put things right when you get them wrong? Moments of connection are worth treasuring, but they come and go. They are not the unit by which love should be measured. How you behave when you don’t feel especially close tells you more about whether you’re going through a hard season or the relationship has run its course.

item.title: Is the Way You Lead Change Wearing You Out?
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Is the Way You Lead Change Wearing You Out?

Most of us have a go-to approach for leading through change. Does yours work?

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • Most of us have a go-to approach to change, and under pressure it's often the one wearing us out.
  • Leaders who are able to adapt are nearly twice as likely to be feeling well as those who try to control.
  • The skill is consciously choosing your approach, telling your team why, and shifting when required.

When the last change landed at work, what did you do first? Try to quickly get it under control? Take more on to try and save others from it? Push back and challenge why it was needed? Or wait and hope it would just blow over?

Whether you consciously chose, or just reacted, we all have a change approach. And when changes keep arriving with little breathing space between them, it's easy to fall into the same approach every time without stopping to ask whether it's still serving you, your team, or your workplace well.

The Five Change Approaches

In our 2026 survey of 380 leaders, five approaches to change stood out. Each has its benefits and its costs. And most of us lean on one more than the rest: 82 percent of the leaders we surveyed named a single go-to. Can you spot which one you favor?

  • Control (36 percent of leaders): You manage the change through tighter planning and oversight. "Run it by me first." When there's a fixed deadline or a safety requirement, ensuring people fall into line and comply can steady everyone. But your team feels watched, waits to be corrected, and accountability slides up to you. Our data found that of the leaders who took this approach, 44 percent rated their changes successful, 23 percent were feeling well, and 40 percent were burning out.

  • Adapt (28 percent of leaders): You sense and adjust as the change unfolds. "What could we try? What help do we need?" When you need people's commitment, this gives you room to learn and grow together as you go, to talk openly and honestly as you navigate challenges, and to build deeper levels of trust. But it costs effort, and the discomfort of slowing down for consultation when every instinct says act now. Our data found that of the leaders who took this approach, 71 percent rated their changes successful, 43 percent were feeling well (the most of any approach), and 23 percent were burning out (the fewest of any approach).

  • Rescue (18 percent of leaders): You work harder, faster, or longer in an effort to save others. "I'll take care of it." When change disrupts, helping to share the load of unexpected demands or smoothing over fraught relationships for a little while is kind. But you pay first, and every problem you absorb robs your team of learning opportunities and teaches them to hand things up to you. Our data found that of the leaders who took this approach, 54 percent rated their changes successful, 14 percent were feeling well, and 50 percent were burning out.

  • Avoid (12 percent of leaders): You keep your distance and let it play out. "Let's wait it out." When the requirements are unclear or conflict with other priorities, holding back can spare people churn. But your team can be left in the dark, rumours fill the silence, and people wait to be told. Our data found that of the leaders who took this approach, 52 percent rated their changes successful, 17 percent were feeling well, and 44 percent were burning out.

  • Resist (3 percent of leaders). You push back and argue for a different approach. "We've tried that before." When a change is not fit for purpose, challenging the thinking early can spare everyone wasted effort and cost. But you carry the fight, and your team gets caught in the middle, hearing the change from above and your objections beside them, and feeling they have to choose sides. Our data found that of the leaders who took this approach, 12 percent rated their changes successful, 0 percent were feeling well, and 78 percent were burning out.

Whichever approach you recognized, it has served you well at some point, which is why you return to it. It helps you feel safe enough when the uncertainty of change arrives. Each approach has its place, and each can be the wrong call for a particular change. The cost shows up when one of them becomes the way you meet every change, whether it fits or not.

Try this: Name your go-to change approach. Then think of the last time it served a change well, and the last time it didn't. What was different?

Which Approach Does This Change Need?

Adapting generally gives you the best odds on both success and well-being. People commit to what they've helped shape. Sensing and adjusting as you go catches what the plan missed before it gets expensive. And the honest conversations build the trust your team will draw on for the next change.

But consultation takes time, energy, and resources you won't always have. When a change has to be complied with quickly to close a risk, control may work best. When it has to be delivered fast, and your team doesn't yet have the skills, rescue may be the smart choice. When it lacks clarity or conflicts with other priorities, avoiding it for a while may pay off. And when it undermines the practices your delivery depends on, resisting is a responsible act.

The skill is making a conscious choice and being willing to shift your approach if needed. The longer control, rescue, avoid, or resist runs, the more it wears on your team and on you. So keep an eye on the clock, and keep asking people how they're doing while you do.

Try this: Tell your team which approach you're taking and why. Then agree on regular check-in dates to ask how the change is landing, whether the approach still fits, and what needs to shift. In our separate 2026 survey of 811 workers, only 26 percent said people on their team often tell the truth about how a change feels, so ask, then listen. You don't have to fix everything they say, and if you can't answer something yet, it's OK to say so.

Which approach are you taking to the change in front of you, and have you told anyone why?
